# VitalityRise — Men's Pelvic Floor Training

VitalityRise (App Store name: Vitality Rise: Men's Health) is an iPhone app for men's pelvic floor training. It runs guided contract-and-relax sessions, pelvic mobility and breathing work, a 30-day plan, and progress scoring. Everything a user enters stays on the device: no account, no cloud sync, no ads. Built by Kyrylo Lozovyi (VITALITY RISE LLC). US pricing: $4.99/week, $9.99/month or $34.99/year (both with a 3-day free trial), or $99.99 once. iOS 17 or later.

It is a general wellness app, not medical care, and does not diagnose or treat erectile dysfunction or any other condition.

Index: https://www.vitalityrize.me/llms.txt

# Pelvic floor training for men, done properly
URL: https://www.vitalityrize.me/
Language: en
Description: A guided pelvic floor trainer for men: timed contract-and-relax sessions, breathing and mobility work, a 30-day plan. Your answers stay on your device.

VitalityRise is an iPhone app that trains the pelvic floor — the muscle
group that sits under the bladder and wraps the base of the penis. It runs the
contract-and-relax timing for you, progresses the difficulty over 30 days, and keeps
what you tell it on your phone.

- No account, ever

- Answers stay on device

- 1–3 minute sessions

- iPhone, iOS 17+

- 22 languages

## What the app actually does

### Guided pelvic floor sessions

Seven sessions that get harder in a deliberate order, from eight rounds of a
3-second squeeze to fourteen rounds of a 6-second squeeze, each with a relax
phase that is at least as long as the squeeze. The ring counts it out so you are
not watching a clock and losing the contraction.

How to do a kegel correctly →

### The relax half, which most apps skip

A pelvic floor that cannot let go is its own problem, and squeezing harder makes
it worse. Every session gives the release its own timed phase and its own cue,
because the muscle has to do both jobs.

Check which problem you have →

### Breathing and hip mobility

Timed breath patterns for arousal control and stress, plus short mobility
routines for the hips and lower back. The pelvic floor does not work in
isolation — it moves with the diaphragm on every breath.

### A 30-day plan, not a library

One day at a time, three phases, four goals a day. Streaks, a history grid that
shows exactly which days you finished, and scores recalculated as you go. No
feed to binge and nothing to browse.

What it was built from →

## What it does not do

VitalityRise is a general wellness app. It is not a treatment, it does not diagnose
anything, and it will not tell you that a muscle exercise fixes every cause of
erectile difficulty — because it doesn't. Erections depend on blood vessels, nerves,
hormones and what is going on in your head, and the pelvic floor is one part of one of
those. What the evidence supports is real but specific, and
the evidence page says exactly
how specific.

There are also no leaderboards, no social features, no ads, and no photographs of
anyone's body. The app is deliberately dull to look at over your shoulder.

## Where to start

- Finding the muscle —
four cues and three checks. Most people get this wrong on the first attempt.

- Kegel exercises for men —
the protocol, and the four mistakes that make it useless.

- Pelvic floor training
and erections — what the randomised trials actually found.

- Losing it partway — a
different problem from never getting one, with a different fix.

- The self-check — weak,
too tight, or something that needs a doctor.

- The kegel apps compared —
including ours, with its weaknesses named.

## Common questions

Q: Is VitalityRise free?
A: The assessment and your baseline scores are free. The 30-day plan and the guided sessions need a subscription: $4.99 a week, $9.99 a month or $34.99 a year — the monthly and yearly plans both start with a 3-day free trial — or $99.99 once for lifetime access. Prices are US App Store prices and vary by country.

Q: Does it work on Android?
A: Not yet. VitalityRise is iPhone-only, iOS 17 or later. There is no web version and no Android build in progress.

Q: Do I need any equipment?
A: No. Pelvic floor training is bodyweight work you can do sitting, standing or lying down, and nobody can tell you are doing it. The app is the timer, the progression and the record.

Q: How long does a session take?
A: Between one and three minutes. The shortest session is eight rounds of a 3-second squeeze; the longest in the plan is fourteen rounds of a 6-second squeeze. The daily plan usually adds a breathing or mobility session on top, so a full day is under ten minutes.

Q: Will this cure erectile dysfunction?
A: No, and any app that says otherwise is selling you something. Pelvic floor training has real trial evidence behind it for erectile function — in the best-known randomised trial, 40% of men regained normal function at six months and another 35.5% improved — but it is one input among many, and persistent ED is a reason to see a doctor rather than an app.

Q: Is my data private?
A: Your assessment answers, scores, streaks and plan progress are stored on your device and are never uploaded. There is no account and no login. The app does send anonymous, hashed usage analytics and privacy-preserving install attribution, which are covered in detail in the privacy policy.

Q: How do I cancel?
A: In iOS Settings → your name → Subscriptions, or in the App Store app under your profile. Cancelling during a 3-day trial costs you nothing. The support page walks through it.

# Who builds VitalityRise
URL: https://www.vitalityrize.me/about/
Language: en
Description: VitalityRise is built by one developer, Kyrylo Lozovyi, trading as VITALITY RISE LLC. No investors, no medical board — and rules the app will not break.

VitalityRise is made by one person. That is worth knowing before you
decide whether to trust anything on this site.

## The person

I'm Kyrylo Lozovyi, an independent iOS developer. I write the code, the copy, the
30-day plan and these pages, and I answer the support email. The company behind the app
is VITALITY RISE LLC, which exists so that Apple has something to pay
and someone to hold responsible.

There are no investors, no growth team, no content agency and no medical advisory
board. Where a bigger company would put a "reviewed by our medical team" badge, this
site puts a linked citation instead — you can check a paper; you cannot check a badge.
Exactly what that means in practice is written down on the
editorial standards page.

I also build Silex, an iPhone app for quitting
gambling, on the same principles: no accounts, no claims to treat anything, every
number sourced. If the approach here looks familiar from there, that is why.

## What the app is

An iPhone app that runs pelvic floor training sessions, breathing and mobility work,
and a 30-day plan, and keeps what you tell it on your phone. It is in the App Store's
Health & Fitness category as a general wellness app. It is not a medical device and
has not been through any regulatory approval process, because it does not do anything
that requires one.

## Rules the app will not break

- No claim to treat or cure anything. Not in the app, not in an ad,
not in an App Store screenshot. The evidence supports something specific and
moderate, and the pages here say exactly how specific.

- No sensitive data leaves your phone. Assessment answers, scores,
check-ins, streaks and plan progress are stored locally and are never uploaded. There
is no account to create and no server holding your answers.

- No dark patterns on the subscription. One price per period, no
add-on packs on top of a subscription, no fake countdowns, and a lifetime option for
people who would rather not subscribe at all. Cancelling is Apple's flow, and the
support page tells you where it is.

- No bodies. No photographs of people, no before-and-after images, no
implied physical outcomes. The app is deliberately dull-looking over your shoulder.

- No leaderboards or sharing. Nothing about this belongs in a feed.

## What I get wrong

The app is new and has almost no reviews. It is iPhone-only with no Android version
planned. The recovery and breathing content is the thinnest-evidenced part of it, and
the methodology page says so. And a one-person app carries a
real risk that a larger one does not: if I stop, it stops. The lifetime purchase exists
partly because that risk should not also cost you a subscription.

## The name

The app is VitalityRise, with an S. The domain is
vitalityrize.me, with a Z, because that is what was available. There is
also an unrelated supplement called VitalRize, which is not us, not affiliated with us,
and not something we have any control over. If you arrived here looking for a pill, this
is the wrong site.

## Contact

Email support@vitalityrize.me for support,
press, a bug, a correction to something on this site, or to tell me the app is wrong
about something. Corrections to the clinical content are especially welcome and will be
made with the update date changed on the page.

## Common questions

Q: Who is behind VitalityRise?
A: Kyrylo Lozovyi, an independent iOS developer, trading as VITALITY RISE LLC. The app is built, written, designed and supported by one person. There is no medical board and no investors.

Q: Is there a doctor involved?
A: No. There is no clinician on the team and the site does not claim one. What the site does instead is cite a named, linked source for every clinical statement, so you can check the claim rather than trust the credential.

Q: Is this the same as the VitalRize supplement?
A: No. VitalRize is an unrelated men's supplement product sold by a different company. VitalityRise is an iPhone app and sells nothing you swallow. The names being similar is an accident and an annoying one.

Q: How do I contact you?
A: support@vitalityrize.me. It goes to one person and gets answered.

# Kegel apps for men, compared
URL: https://www.vitalityrize.me/best-kegel-apps-for-men/
Language: en
Description: Dr. Kegel, Squeezy Men, Kegel Men, Better P, Kegel Trainer and VitalityRise: what each costs and which to pick. Disclosure — we make one of them.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-09-18

Short answer: All of these apps do the same core thing — time a squeeze, time a release, count the rounds — and no app can tell whether you are contracting the right muscle. So pick on price, tolerance for upselling, and whether the app trains release as well as squeeze. Dr. Kegel has by far the largest user base. Squeezy Men is the one designed by NHS physiotherapists, and costs $4.99 once. Kegel Trainer is the cheapest credible option and is not men-specific. Better P is the most expensive. VitalityRise — ours — is the only one here that offers a one-time lifetime purchase, and the newest, with no rating history to judge it by.

Disclosure: we make VitalityRise, one of the apps in this table.
That is a reason to read our entry sceptically, so we have listed its weaknesses
alongside everything else's. Every price below was read from each app's own US App
Store listing on 18 September 2026 — we take no affiliate commission from any of these
links, and there are no affiliate links on this page.

There are dozens of these apps and they are much more alike than their marketing
suggests. All of them time a contraction, time a release, count rounds, and draw a
streak. The differences that actually affect whether you get anything out of one are
narrow, so this page leads with them.

Several of these apps list many concurrent price points for the same product, which is

## What actually distinguishes them

### Whether the app trains release

A pelvic floor that will not relax causes pain, urinary hesitancy and, for some men,
worse sexual function — and it is a real risk of enthusiastic unsupervised training.
Apps that treat the release as dead time between squeezes teach the wrong pattern. Look
for a relax phase that is timed, cued and at least as long as the hold.

### How hard it upsells

Two of the apps above sell add-on packs on top of a subscription. That is worth
weighing, because the whole product is a few minutes of timed contractions and there is
no feature in this category worth $39.90 on top of what you already paid.

### Whether it is a plan or a library

An open library of exercises leaves you deciding what to do today, which is the
decision most people get wrong or skip. A fixed progression removes it. This is
preference, not evidence — but if you have abandoned exercise apps before, it is
usually here.

### What none of them do

None of these apps can tell whether you are contracting the pelvic floor or your
buttocks. The trial that produced the good erectile function numbers used manometric
biofeedback and a physiotherapist for exactly that reason. If you are unsure about
technique, the highest-value thing you can buy is not an app — it is one session with a
pelvic health physiotherapist.

## How to choose

- You want the largest, most-reviewed option: Dr. Kegel.

- You want to spend as little as possible: Kegel Trainer, or no app
at all and the protocol on the kegel page with
your phone's timer — everything on this site is free to read.

- You want it designed by clinicians: Squeezy Men — and it is the
cheapest thing here that is actually built for men.

- You would rather buy once than subscribe: Squeezy Men or Kegel
Trainer's unlock at the low end, VitalityRise's lifetime at the high end.

- You want a fixed 30-day plan and no add-on selling: VitalityRise,
with the caveat that it is new and unproven in the market.

If you have already tried the category leader and want out, the
Dr. Kegel alternatives page goes app by app.

## Common questions

Q: Do kegel apps actually work?
A: The app is a timer and a habit device; the exercise is what works, and only when the technique is right. The clinical trial that produced the good numbers for erectile dysfunction used a physiotherapist and a manometric biofeedback device — neither of which any of these apps replicate. If you will do the protocol without an app, you lose nothing by not buying one.

Q: What is the best free kegel app for men?
A: There is no genuinely free option among the men's apps: they are free downloads with the training behind a subscription, or a small one-time price. The cheapest credible one-time purchases are Squeezy Men ($4.99, physiotherapist-designed) and Kegel Trainer's unlocks ($2.99, not men-specific). The actual free option is a phone timer and the protocol on our kegel page.

Q: Why are these apps so expensive?
A: Because they are sold through onboarding funnels that qualify a motivated user and then present a subscription, and because the category converts well. Several of the apps here list five or more concurrent price points for the same product, which is what running continuous price tests looks like from the outside. Assume the price you see is the price you were assigned, not the price.

Q: Which kegel app has the most users?
A: Dr. Kegel: For Men's Health, with over 45,000 App Store ratings in the US at the time of writing — an order of magnitude more than anything else in the men's category.

Q: Does an app help more than just doing kegels myself?
A: Only in the two ways any exercise app helps: it removes the decision about what to do today, and it makes skipping visible. If those are your failure points, an app earns its money. If your failure point is technique, none of these fixes it and a pelvic health physiotherapist would.

# Cycling and erectile dysfunction
URL: https://www.vitalityrize.me/cycling-and-erectile-dysfunction/
Language: en
Description: A study of nearly 4,000 athletes found cyclists no worse off than swimmers or runners. Numbness is the signal that matters, and it is fixable.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: Mostly no. A large multinational study comparing cyclists with swimmers and runners found no worse sexual function in the cyclists — and the cardiovascular benefit of riding works in the opposite direction, since aerobic exercise is the best-evidenced non-drug intervention for erectile function there is. What does track with trouble is genital numbness: a marker of perineal compression, associated with worse scores, and largely fixable with saddle and position changes. Numbness is the signal. Riding, by itself, is not.

This is one of those health claims that circulates permanently and is rarely checked against
the research. The short version: the risk is real, narrower than the folklore, and mostly
about pressure rather than about cycling.

## What the large studies found

Awad and colleagues surveyed a large, multinational sample of athletes and compared cyclists
with swimmers and runners on sexual and urinary function. Nearly 4,000 responses. The
cyclists did not have worse sexual function than the other athletes.

That is a cross-sectional survey rather than a trial, with all the usual caveats about
self-selection and self-report. But it is a large sample with a sensible comparison group —
other endurance athletes rather than the general population — and it is the best answer
available to the plain question.

The companion finding is the more useful one. In a related large study, bicycle-related
genital numbness was associated with worse scores on the Sexual Health Inventory for
Men. Not riding. Numbness.

## The mechanism, and why the distinction matters

The perineum — the area between the sit bones — carries the pudendal nerve and the internal
pudendal artery, which between them supply sensation and blood to the penis. A saddle that
puts your weight there instead of on your sit bones compresses both. Sustained compression
reduces blood flow and irritates the nerve, and the immediate result is the numbness cyclists
know well.

So the causal chain runs through pressure, not through pedalling. Two riders doing identical
mileage can have completely different perineal loads depending on saddle, fit and posture,
which is exactly why "does cycling cause ED" gets a muddy answer at the population level while
the numbness question gets a clear one.

## The other half of the ledger

Cycling is aerobic exercise, and aerobic exercise is the single best-evidenced non-drug
intervention for erectile function. The systematic review evidence points to roughly 160
minutes a week of moderate-to-vigorous activity improving erectile function in men whose
difficulty is vascular or metabolic — which is most men whose difficulty is physical at all.

Quitting cycling to protect your erections therefore has a good chance of achieving the
opposite. The exercise evidence in
full →

## What to actually change

- Treat numbness as a stop signal. Not something to push through, not
something that toughens up. If you go numb, the setup is wrong.

- Get your sit bones measured. Most bike shops do it in two minutes. A
saddle narrower than your sit-bone spacing forces load onto soft tissue no matter what
shape it is.

- Consider a cut-out or noseless saddle. Both reduce measured perineal
pressure. Neither is magic, and fit still dominates.

- Level the saddle. A nose-up tilt drives pressure straight into the
perineum. Level, or very slightly nose-down, is the usual fix.

- Check the bar height. An aggressive low position rotates the pelvis
forward and shifts you off the sit bones. This is why the problem is commoner on road bikes
in a racing position than on upright bikes.

- Stand up regularly. Out of the saddle for ten to twenty seconds every ten
minutes or so restores flow and costs nothing.

- Break up very long rides. Risk concentrates in duration and cumulative
pressure, not in whether you ride at all.

## The pelvic floor angle

Long hours in the saddle are also one of the contributors to a chronically tight pelvic
floor, via sustained pressure and the hip flexor shortening that comes with a seated,
forward-rotated position. If you ride a lot and have perineal pain, urinary hesitancy or pain
after ejaculation — rather than simple numbness during rides — that is a different picture and
strengthening exercises will make it worse.
What that looks like and what helps →

## Sources

- Awad MA, Gaither TW, Murphy GP, et al. Cycling, and male sexual and urinary function: results from a large,
multinational, cross-sectional study. J Urol 2018;199(3):798–804.

- Baradaran N, Awad M, Gaither TW, et al. The association of
bicycle-related genital numbness and Sexual Health Inventory for Men (SHIM) score: results
from a large, multinational, cross-sectional study. BJU Int
2019;124(2):336–341.

- Gerbild H, Larsen CM, Graugaard C, Areskoug Josefsson K. Physical activity to
improve erectile function: a systematic review of intervention studies. Sex Med
2018;6(2):75–89.

## Common questions

Q: Does cycling cause erectile dysfunction?
A: The largest comparison available found no significant difference in sexual function between cyclists and other athletes such as swimmers and runners. The concern is not baseless — the perineum takes load on a saddle, and pudendal nerve and arterial compression are real mechanisms — but at typical recreational volumes the population-level effect has not shown up. Very long durations, high saddle pressure and poor fit are where risk concentrates.

Q: Why do I go numb on the bike?
A: Because your weight is on the perineum instead of your sit bones. The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal artery run through that area, and sustained pressure compresses both. Numbness is the nerve telling you the pressure is too high for too long — it is the most reliable warning sign in this whole topic and should not be ridden through.

Q: Is genital numbness while cycling dangerous?
A: It is a signal to act on rather than an emergency. Numbness during riding is associated with worse Sexual Health Inventory for Men scores, and it usually resolves when the pressure does. Persistent numbness that lasts well after riding is a reason to change your setup now and to see a doctor if it does not settle.

Q: What saddle stops numbness?
A: Whichever one puts your weight on the sit bones rather than the soft tissue between them. Cut-outs and noseless designs both reduce measured perineal pressure, but fit is individual and saddle width relative to your sit-bone spacing matters more than the shape marketing. Get measured at a bike shop rather than guessing.

Q: Should I stop cycling if I have ED?
A: Almost certainly not. Aerobic exercise has the strongest evidence of any non-drug intervention for erectile function, so stopping is likely to make things worse overall. Change the saddle, the fit and the habits first, and reassess.

Q: How long does cycling numbness take to go away?
A: Usually minutes to hours after you get off, once the compression stops. Numbness that persists for days, or that appears when you are not riding, is a different matter and worth a medical opinion.

# Dr. Kegel: review and alternatives
URL: https://www.vitalityrize.me/dr-kegel-alternatives/
Language: en
Description: An honest Dr. Kegel review — 45,000 ratings, eight price points — and the alternatives by what each does better, including when Dr. Kegel is still right.
Published: 2026-09-18 · Updated: 2026-09-18

Short answer: Dr. Kegel is the biggest men's pelvic floor app by a wide margin — 45,000+ US ratings — and its weaknesses are the ones size produces: eight concurrent price points from $4.99 a week to $59.99 a year, decided by the funnel you land in, and no way to buy it once. If you want clinician-designed, Squeezy Men ($4.99 once, NHS physiotherapists). If you want the cheapest credible timer, Kegel Trainer. If you want a fixed 30-day plan with a lifetime price and no add-ons, ours — with the caveat that we are new and have no ratings. If you want the most users and the most polish and don't mind the pricing, Dr. Kegel is still the answer.

Disclosure: we make VitalityRise, one of the apps below. Every price
and rating on this page was read from the app's own US App Store listing on 18 September
2026, no affiliate links, and our own entry lists its weaknesses in the same terms as
everyone else's.

Dr. Kegel: For Men's Health is the category leader and it is not close — over 45,000 US
ratings against under 10,000 for the next largest. If you are looking for an alternative, it
is usually for one of three reasons, and the right alternative depends on which.

## Dr. Kegel, reviewed

What it does well is real. It is the most polished app in the category, it has the widest
feature set, and with 45,000 ratings it is the one most likely to still exist in five years
— which matters more for a habit app than any single feature. If you have not tried it and
the pricing does not bother you, it is a reasonable default. Where it loses people:

- The pricing. Eight concurrent in-app purchases are listed: a $9.99
"1-week trial", $4.99 weekly, two monthly plans ($12.99 and $19.99), a $29.99 3-month plan,
and three yearly plans ($29.99, $56.99, $59.99). That is not a price list; it is the
visible surface of a price test, and what you pay depends on the onboarding variant you were
assigned.

- No one-time option. Everything is a subscription.

- The polish is the product. It is a very well-built consumer app. Some
men want something plainer, cheaper, or designed by someone with a clinical background.

## The alternatives, by what they do better

### Squeezy Men — clinician-designed, one price

$4.99 once. Living With Ltd. 4.62 on 45 US ratings; 4.77 on 1,125 in the UK.

Designed by chartered NHS physiotherapists specialising in men's health, according to its
own listing, and built to run a programme a clinician has set — which makes it the obvious
choice if you are already seeing a physiotherapist and want the app to follow their plan
rather than its own. Its listing also says something no other app here says: that men
should only be doing these exercises if they have symptoms or are around a prostatectomy.
That is the most conservative position in the category and, given the evidence, not an
unreasonable one.

The trade: it is a UK app with a small US user base, and it is a tool rather than a
programme. It will time what your physiotherapist told you to do. It will not tell you what
to do.

### Kegel Trainer PFM Exercises — cheapest, oldest, not men-specific

$2.99/mo, $9.99/6mo, $19.99/yr, or one-time unlocks from $2.99. Olson Applications.
4.84 on 8,196 US ratings.

The lowest credible prices in the category and the longest track record. The trade is that
it is a general pelvic floor trainer: nothing in it is aimed at erectile function or
ejaculatory control, and the framing is not written for men. If all you want is a reliable
timer with progression and you already know the protocol, it does that job for less than
anything else.

### Kegel Men — the closest like-for-like

$9.99–$19.99/mo, $19.99–$44.99/6mo, $23.99–$59.99/yr, plus paid add-ons.
4.62 on 9,583 US ratings.

The nearest thing to Dr. Kegel in shape and size, which is both the case for it and the case
against. It has the same funnel-driven pricing (ten listed purchases) and adds separate paid
packs on top of the subscription — a $39.90 "AI" coach and a $19.90 tips pack. If your reason
for leaving Dr. Kegel was pricing, this does not solve it.

### VitalityRise — ours: a plan, one price, lifetime option

$4.99/wk, $9.99/mo, $34.99/yr, or $99.99 lifetime. VITALITY RISE LLC. No
ratings yet.

Built around a fixed 30-day programme rather than an open library, with one price per
period, no add-on purchases, and a lifetime option for people who would rather not
subscribe. Every session times the release phase as deliberately as the squeeze, because a
pelvic floor that cannot let go is its own problem.

The honest case against: it is new, it has no rating history, it is iPhone-only, and it is
built by one person — if longevity matters to you, that is a real mark against it, and it is
the main reason the lifetime price exists. What it actually does →

### Better P — the expensive one

$19.99/mo, $39.99/12wk, $59.99/6mo, $99.99/yr. Appinity. 4.67 on 440 US
ratings.

The highest yearly price in the category with no lifetime option. Hard to make the case for
it over Dr. Kegel on price, or over Squeezy Men on credentials, or over ours on structure.
Included because it is often listed, not because we would pick it.

You are seeing a physiotherapist alreadySqueezy Men — it runs their programme

You want the most users and most polishStay with Dr. Kegel

## What none of them change

The exercise is the same in every app, and the thing the clinical trial had that no app has
is a physiotherapist checking whether you were contracting the right muscle. Before you
change apps, check that: the four cues and
three checks. If technique is the problem, no app on this page fixes it, and one session
with a pelvic health physiotherapist would.

The full comparison table, with every price →

## Common questions

Q: Is there a free alternative to Dr. Kegel?
A: Not a genuinely free men's app — every one in the category is a free download with training behind a paywall, or a small one-time price. The closest to free are Squeezy Men at $4.99 once and Kegel Trainer's $2.99 unlocks. Genuinely free is a phone timer and the protocol on our kegel page, which is what the apps are timing anyway.

Q: What is the best one-time purchase kegel app for men?
A: Squeezy Men ($4.99, designed by NHS physiotherapists) is the strongest one-time option built specifically for men. Kegel Trainer offers one-time unlocks from $2.99 but is a general pelvic floor app. VitalityRise offers a $99.99 lifetime purchase at the other end of the range, with a fixed 30-day programme behind it.

Q: Why does Dr. Kegel show different prices to different people?
A: Its listing carries eight concurrent in-app purchases for what is essentially one product, including a $9.99 '1-week trial'. That is what continuous price testing looks like from the outside: the price you are offered depends on which onboarding variant you were assigned, not on a list price. It is not unique to Dr. Kegel — Kegel Men lists ten — but it is most visible on the largest app.

Q: Does any kegel app work better than another?
A: No app can tell whether you are contracting the right muscle, and the clinical trial that produced the good erectile-function numbers used a physiotherapist and a biofeedback device that none of these apps replicate. The apps differ in price, in whether they train release as well as squeeze, in how hard they upsell, and in whether they give you a plan or a library. They do not differ in what the exercise does.

Q: Is Dr. Kegel worth it?
A: If you want the app the most men use, with the most polish and the widest feature set, and you are comfortable with subscription pricing that varies, then yes. Its size is a real advantage — it will still exist next year, which is not something a one-person app can promise. The reasons to look elsewhere are price structure, wanting a one-time purchase, or wanting something designed by clinicians rather than by a growth team.

Q: Is VitalityRise a good Dr. Kegel alternative?
A: We make it, so read this sceptically. It is a fixed 30-day plan rather than a library, has one price per period with no add-on purchases, offers a lifetime option, and times the release phase as deliberately as the squeeze. It is also new, iPhone-only, has no rating history, and is built by one person. Whether that trade is right for you depends on how much you value longevity versus structure.

# Editorial standards
URL: https://www.vitalityrize.me/editorial-standards/
Language: en
Description: No medical reviewer, so the process has to do the work: how every clinical figure is verified, how corrections happen, and the things this site will not do.

This site has no medical reviewer. That is a real gap, and it is stated on
every page rather than papered over. What follows is what the site does instead, written
down so it can be held to it.

## Every clinical number is traced to a paper you can open

Not "studies show". Not "research suggests". A named trial, its authors, journal, year and
page numbers, with a link — usually a DOI, sometimes a PubMed record. If a claim cannot be
tied to a specific paper, it is either labelled as clinical consensus or it is not made.

The figures that carry the most weight on this site — 40% regaining normal erectile
function at six months, 35.5% improving, 24.5% not; 31.7 seconds to 146.2 in the premature
ejaculation study; formal training no better than standard care after prostate surgery —
each sit next to the paper they came from, and the paper's own limitations are stated in the
same section. The 24.5% who did not improve is on the page next to the 40% who did.

## Citations are verified, not remembered

Before a citation goes live, the author list, journal, year, volume and pages are checked
against Crossref or PubMed. This sounds obvious. It is not standard practice, and the reason
it is written here is that during the first build of this site a review's author list was
drafted from memory, turned out to be wrong, and was caught by exactly this check. The rule
exists because it was needed.

## The evidence's weakness is part of the claim

A single trial of 55 men is described as a single trial of 55 men. An uncontrolled study is
called uncontrolled, with an explanation of why that matters. Where the evidence is
contested — pornography and erectile function is the clearest case — the page says what is
established, what is plausible, and what is advocacy, and links neither advocacy camp.

## Commercial conflicts are disclosed on the page, not in a footer

We make one of the apps in this category. The
comparison page says so above the table, lists our
weaknesses in the same columns as everyone else's, takes no affiliate commission, and reads
every competitor's price from that vendor's own App Store listing on a stated date. The
prostate surgery page says the app is
the wrong tool for that population, because the evidence says so.

## Structured data describes what is true

No aggregateRating until the app has enough real ratings to report one. No
reviewer in the schema when there is no reviewer. No MedicalScholarlyArticle
markup on pages that are not scholarly articles. Search engines are told exactly what a
reader is told.

## Corrections change the date

Every article carries a published date and an updated date. A correction updates the second
one. If a correction changes a conclusion rather than a detail, the text says what changed.
Send corrections to support@vitalityrize.me;
the clinical pages are where they are most welcome.

## What the site will not do

- Claim to treat, cure or diagnose anything, in any language.

- Present a projection as a measurement, or an internal score as a clinical scale.

- Recommend supplements or testosterone products.

- Put a "medically reviewed" line on a page nobody medically reviewed.

- Use before-and-after imagery, photographs of bodies, or implied physical outcomes.

- Quote a recovery timeline that comes from a forum rather than a trial.

## Who writes it

Kyrylo Lozovyi, who also builds the app. One person, no editorial
team, and no pretence of one. The methodology page lists every
source the programme was built from and the parts of the app we would cut first if forced to
justify each screen.

## Common questions

Q: Who checks the medical claims on this site?
A: No clinician does, and the site says so rather than implying otherwise. What replaces a reviewer is process: every clinical figure is traced to a named, linked paper, and the citation itself — authors, journal, year, pages — is verified against Crossref or PubMed before publishing, not recalled from memory. You can check the paper; you cannot check a badge.

Q: Why not just get a doctor to review it?
A: Because a name on a page is only worth what the person actually did, and most 'medically reviewed by' lines on health sites mean a fee and a skim. A real review by a pelvic health physiotherapist would improve the four clinical pages, and we would rather have none than a decorative one. If that changes, the reviewer's name, credential and what they reviewed will appear on the page.

Q: What happens when something is wrong?
A: It gets fixed, the page's updated date changes, and if the correction changes a conclusion the old version is described in the text rather than silently overwritten. Corrections go to support@vitalityrize.me and are the most useful email the site receives.

Q: Does the app company influence the content?
A: The app company is one person, and he writes the content, so yes — completely. The mitigation is stated rather than hidden: the comparison page discloses that we make one of the apps, lists our weaknesses in the same table as everyone else's, and the prostate surgery page says outright that the app is the wrong tool for that. Where honesty and conversion conflict, the site is built to choose honesty, and you can check whether it did.

# Erectile dysfunction without medication
URL: https://www.vitalityrize.me/erectile-dysfunction-without-medication/
Language: en
Description: Aerobic exercise, weight, sleep, smoking, alcohol and pelvic floor training, ranked by the evidence behind each — plus what does not work.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: The interventions with the best evidence are unglamorous and physical. Aerobic exercise has the strongest support — roughly 160 minutes a week of moderate-to-vigorous activity over six months meaningfully improves erectile function in men whose ED comes from inactivity, obesity, hypertension, metabolic syndrome or cardiovascular disease. Weight loss, stopping smoking and treating sleep apnoea come next. Pelvic floor training has one good randomised trial behind it. Testosterone boosters and most supplements have nothing.

Everything on this page is ranked the same way: how good is the evidence, and how much
difference does it make. Nothing is included because it sounds healthy.

## 1. Aerobic exercise — the strongest evidence

Gerbild and colleagues reviewed the intervention studies and concluded that supervised
aerobic activity of moderate to vigorous intensity, performed at least four times a
week for at least 40 minutes, is an effective tool in the management of erectile
dysfunction. Roughly 160 minutes a week for six months reduced erectile
problems in men whose ED stemmed from physical inactivity, obesity, hypertension,
metabolic syndrome or cardiovascular disease.

The mechanism is not mysterious. Erections require healthy endothelium — the lining of
blood vessels — and aerobic exercise is one of the few things that reliably improves
it. This is also why the benefit is concentrated in men whose ED is vascular: if your
blood vessels are fine, improving them further does less.

"Moderate to vigorous" means you are breathing hard enough that talking in full
sentences is work. Brisk walking counts if you are unfit; it stops counting once you
are not.

## 2. Losing weight, if there is weight to lose

Abdominal fat is metabolically active tissue that converts testosterone to oestrogen
and drives the insulin resistance and inflammation behind vascular disease. Weight-loss
trials in men with obesity and ED show erectile function improving roughly in
proportion to the weight lost. This overlaps heavily with the exercise evidence, which
is a reason to do both rather than to pick one.

## 3. Stopping smoking

Nicotine is a vasoconstrictor and smoking accelerates atherosclerosis, so it damages
erections through both the acute and the chronic route. Improvement after quitting is
well documented and is faster in younger men and men who smoked for fewer years.

## 4. Sleep, and specifically sleep apnoea

Obstructive sleep apnoea is strongly associated with erectile dysfunction, plausibly
through nocturnal hypoxia, sympathetic overdrive and suppressed testosterone. It is
also badly underdiagnosed. Loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, waking
unrefreshed and daytime sleepiness are the flags; treating it improves erectile
function in a substantial fraction of affected men. Testosterone is also produced
largely during sleep, which is the more general reason short sleep shows up in this
literature. It is also why morning erections thin out when
you sleep badly, and why that makes them a noisier signal than they first appear.

## 5. Alcohol

Acutely, alcohol is a depressant that impairs the reflex. Chronically, heavy drinking
damages nerves and the liver and lowers testosterone. The dose-response is real: this
is one where cutting back rather than stopping is a legitimate intervention.

## 6. Pelvic floor training

One good randomised trial: 40% of men regained normal erectile function at six months
and 35.5% improved. It is the only item on this list that targets the mechanical rather
than the vascular side, and it is particularly relevant if your complaint is losing
rigidity partway rather than never achieving it.

The trial, in detail →

Two adjacent questions that come up constantly and deserve their own answers:
whether porn is causing this and
whether cycling is.

## 7. Reviewing your medication

Not a lifestyle change, but it belongs here because it is frequently the whole answer.
SSRIs, beta blockers, thiazide diuretics, finasteride and several antipsychotics cause
erectile dysfunction directly. If your ED began within a few months of starting
something, that is the first thing to raise with whoever prescribed it — often there is
an alternative in the same class without the effect. Do not stop anything on your own.

## What does not have the evidence

- Over-the-counter testosterone boosters. No good trial support. Some
products in this category have been found adulterated with undeclared PDE5
inhibitors, which is genuinely dangerous if you take nitrates.

- Most herbal supplements. A few — panax ginseng, L-arginine — have
small studies pointing at modest effects. None have anything resembling the evidence
base of exercise, and supplement quality control is poor.

- Shockwave therapy. Promising early trials, still investigational,
and priced far ahead of its evidence in most clinics offering it.

- "Detoxes", jelqing, penis pumps as a treatment. No. Vacuum devices
do have a legitimate medical use, prescribed and supervised, mostly after prostate
surgery — that is a different thing from the products sold online.

## An honest ordering

If you did exactly one thing from this page, do the aerobic exercise. If you did two,
add the pelvic floor training, because it is five minutes a day and stacks with
everything else. If you did three, get your blood pressure and cholesterol checked —
not because it improves erections, but because your erection may be telling you
something more important than what you asked it.

## Sources

- Gerbild H, Larsen CM, Graugaard C, Areskoug Josefsson K. Physical activity to
improve erectile function: a systematic review of intervention studies. Sex
Med 2018;6(2):75–89.

- Dorey G, Speakman MJ, Feneley RCL, Swinkels A, Dunn CDR. Pelvic floor
exercises for erectile dysfunction. BJU Int 2005;96(4):595–597.

- Montorsi F, Briganti A, Salonia A, et al. Erectile dysfunction
prevalence, time of onset and association with risk factors in 300 consecutive
patients with acute chest pain and angiographically documented coronary artery
disease. Eur Urol 2003;44(3):360–364.

## Common questions

Q: What is the single most effective non-drug treatment for ED?
A: Aerobic exercise, in men whose ED has a vascular or metabolic cause. The systematic review evidence points to at least four sessions a week of 40 minutes at moderate to vigorous intensity, sustained for six months — about 160 minutes a week. It works because it treats the endothelial dysfunction that is causing the problem, rather than working around it.

Q: Can erectile dysfunction be reversed naturally?
A: Sometimes, depending entirely on the cause. ED driven by inactivity, weight, blood pressure, smoking or alcohol frequently improves substantially when those change. ED driven by nerve damage, advanced vascular disease or medication side effects generally does not respond to lifestyle change alone.

Q: Does quitting porn fix erectile dysfunction?
A: For a specific and probably small group of men, reducing high-frequency use appears to help — the mechanism proposed is conditioned arousal to a narrow, novel stimulus. The research base is thin and largely observational, and the online claims run far ahead of it. Worth trying if it fits your pattern; not worth treating as established.

Q: Do testosterone boosters help erectile dysfunction?
A: Over-the-counter 'testosterone boosters' have essentially no good evidence, and several have been found to contain undeclared pharmaceutical ingredients. Genuinely low testosterone is a diagnosis made with a morning blood test and treated by a doctor. If low libido and fatigue arrived with your ED, ask for the test rather than buying the supplement.

Q: How long does it take for lifestyle changes to improve erections?
A: The exercise trials measured at three and six months. Weight loss studies show improvement tracking with the weight lost over a similar period. Nothing here works in a fortnight, which is exactly why the supplement industry exists.

Q: Is ED a sign of something serious?
A: It can be. Erectile dysfunction precedes a coronary event by an average of about three years because the penile arteries are narrower than the coronary ones and clog first. New ED in a man over forty is a reason for a blood pressure check and a lipid panel, not just a reason to buy an app.

# How long do kegels take to work?
URL: https://www.vitalityrize.me/how-long-do-kegels-take-to-work/
Language: en
Description: Nothing for a month, something at six to twelve weeks, the full trial effect at six months. What changes when, and when to conclude it isn't working.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: Expect nothing for the first three to four weeks. The trials that found benefit measured at three and six months, and the men who improved trained daily throughout. Realistic milestones: better awareness and control by week 4, noticeable ejaculatory control around weeks 8–12, erectile changes between 3 and 6 months. If twelve weeks of consistent, correct practice has produced nothing at all, the problem is technique or the cause isn't muscular — and either way, more reps is the wrong response.

This is the most common question about pelvic floor training and the one the marketing
answers worst. "Results in two weeks" is a sales claim. Here is what the research timeline
actually looks like, and what you should expect to notice at each point.

## The honest timeline

WhenWhat changes

Week 1–2
You learn to find and isolate the muscle. Nothing else. If you feel a difference in
function this early, it is expectation rather than tissue.

Week 3–4
Control improves: cleaner contraction, longer hold without recruiting glutes or
abdominals, more complete release. This is genuine progress and is not an outcome.

Week 6–8
First functional changes for some men — usually ejaculatory control, occasionally
less post-void dribbling. Muscle adaptation is real by now.

Week 8–12
The window in which most responders in the premature ejaculation study were
improving. Erectile changes may begin.

3 months
The first fair assessment point. In the Dorey trial the training group was
significantly ahead of controls here (p < 0.001).

6 months
The full effect: 40% of men back to normal erectile function, 35.5% improved,
24.5% unchanged.

## Why it is slow

Two reasons, and neither is avoidable.

The first is ordinary muscle physiology. Early strength gains in any muscle are largely
neural — you get better at recruiting what you already have — and only later does the tissue
itself change. The pelvic floor is no exception, and it starts from a worse place than most
muscles because almost nobody has ever trained it deliberately.

The second is that the outcome you care about is downstream of the muscle. Better
contraction has to translate into better venous compression, which has to translate into
better-maintained rigidity, which has to happen often enough for you to notice a pattern.
Each of those steps adds lag.

## What to do at each checkpoint

### Week 4: check technique, not results

Nothing should have changed functionally, so judging outcomes now tells you nothing. Judge
the contraction instead. Use the mirror test: a correct contraction visibly retracts the base
of the penis and lifts the testicles, with the stomach, buttocks and thighs completely still.
If you cannot see that, the next eight weeks will not work, and fixing it now is the highest
return available. The technique checks →

### Week 12: the real decision point

Twelve weeks of consistent, correct daily practice with no change at all is meaningful
information. It usually means one of:

- The technique was wrong all along — the commonest answer, and the reason
the clinical trial used a physiotherapist and a biofeedback device rather than a leaflet.

- The cause isn't muscular. Vascular, hormonal, medication-related or
psychological ED does not respond to this, no matter how well you do it.
What else has evidence →

- The pelvic floor was too tight, not too weak. If twelve weeks of training
has made pain, urgency or hesitancy worse, stop.
That is a different problem with an opposite
treatment →

What it does not mean is that you should do more repetitions. This is a small muscle that
fatigues quickly, and an over-trained pelvic floor generates its own problems.

### After 6 months: maintenance

Detraining is real, so the gains need some ongoing input — but not the full daily programme
forever. Dropping to a few sets a week holds what you built, in the same way that no lifter
keeps adding weight indefinitely.

## What "consistent" means

The trials trained daily. Not "most days when I remember" — daily, for months, which is
exactly why an app exists for this at all. The exercise is free and takes three minutes; the
hard part is doing it four hundred times without a reason to.

That is the only thing VitalityRise is actually for: it removes the decision about what to
do today, counts the rounds, progresses the difficulty on a schedule, and makes skipping
visible. It cannot make the exercise work faster, and it cannot tell you whether you are
contracting the right muscle.

## Sources

- Dorey G, Speakman M, Feneley R, Swinkels A, Dunn C, Ewings P. Randomised controlled trial of
pelvic floor muscle exercises and manometric biofeedback for erectile dysfunction.
Br J Gen Pract 2004;54(508):819–825.

- Dorey G, Speakman MJ, Feneley RCL, Swinkels A, Dunn CDR. Pelvic floor
exercises for erectile dysfunction. BJU Int 2005;96(4):595–597.

- Pastore AL, Palleschi G, Fuschi A, et al. Pelvic floor muscle
rehabilitation for patients with lifelong premature ejaculation. Ther Adv Urol
2014;6(3):83–88.

## Common questions

Q: How long before kegels improve erections?
A: Three months before you can fairly judge it, six for the full effect seen in the research. In the Dorey trial, assessment at three months already showed the training group significantly ahead of controls, and the headline outcome — 40% back to normal function — came from the blinded six-month assessment. Nobody in that trial got there in a fortnight.

Q: How long do kegels take to help premature ejaculation?
A: The pelvic floor rehabilitation study in men with lifelong premature ejaculation ran twelve weeks, and most of the men who responded were improving by around week eight. Average time to ejaculation went from about 32 seconds to about 146 seconds over the full twelve weeks.

Q: Why am I not seeing results from kegels?
A: Three usual reasons, in order. Technique — squeezing the buttocks and abdomen instead of the pelvic floor is extremely common and produces nothing. Consistency — a few sets a week is not the intervention the trials tested. And cause — if your erectile difficulty is vascular, hormonal, medication-related or anxiety-driven, a muscle exercise will not address it however well you do it.

Q: Can you feel kegels working?
A: You feel control before you see results. Within a couple of weeks most men notice they can isolate the contraction more precisely, hold it longer without other muscles joining in, and release it more completely. That is real progress and it is not yet an outcome — it is the prerequisite for one.

Q: Do you have to do kegels forever?
A: To keep the benefit, largely yes — it behaves like any other muscle training, and detraining is real. The practical version is that the daily programme gets you the change and a substantially lighter maintenance dose holds it, in the same way that nobody keeps adding weight to a lift forever.

Q: Is it too late to start if I'm over 60?
A: No. The best-known trial had a median participant age of 59 and a range up to 78, so older men were well represented among those who improved. Age changes the odds, not the eligibility.

# Finding your pelvic floor muscles
URL: https://www.vitalityrize.me/how-to-find-pelvic-floor-muscles-men/
Language: en
Description: Four ways to locate the right muscle, three ways to confirm you have it, and the reason most men spend months squeezing their buttocks instead.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: Four cues, in order of reliability: stop your urine stream once (then never practise there again), watch in a mirror for the base of the penis retracting and the testicles lifting, put a hand on the perineum and feel it tighten, or imagine stopping yourself breaking wind. The confirmation that matters is negative: your stomach, buttocks and thighs must not move, and your breathing must not stop. Almost everyone gets this wrong first go, and the ones who never fix it get nothing out of months of training.

Every study of pelvic floor training runs into the same problem: a large share of people
cannot perform the contraction correctly from verbal instruction alone. That is why the trial
with the good erectile function results used a physiotherapist and a manometric biofeedback
device rather than a leaflet — the checking was the intervention as much as the exercise was.

You do not have either of those. So this page is the substitute: four ways in, and three ways
to verify.

## Four cues to find it

### 1. The urine stream — once

Mid-flow, stop the stream. Whatever you just did was the pelvic floor. This is the most
unambiguous cue there is, because the feedback is instant and unmistakable.

Do it once. Practising kegels while urinating, as a habit, can leave
residual urine in the bladder and irritate it. It is a way of learning the sensation, not a
place to train.

### 2. The mirror

Stand naked in front of a mirror and try to draw the base of the penis inward and the
testicles upward. A correct contraction produces a small but visible movement: the base
retracts slightly, the testicles lift.

This becomes your long-term check, because you can repeat it any time without involving your
bladder, and because it shows you the error as well as the action — if anything else on your
body moves, you can see it.

### 3. The hand on the perineum

Place a couple of fingers on the perineum, the area between the scrotum and the anus, and
contract. You should feel it tighten and draw upward under your fingers.

This is the most useful cue for men who cannot tell from internal sensation alone whether
anything is happening — which, at the start, is a lot of men.

### 4. The wind cue

Imagine you are about to break wind in a crowded room and are trying to stop it. That is the
back half of the same muscle group. It works for people the other cues don't reach, with one
caveat: used alone it tends to recruit the anal sphincter and glutes rather than the front
portion that matters for sexual function. Use it to find the area, then refine with the
mirror.

## The three checks that matter more

Finding it is easier than not doing something else at the same time. Every one of these is a
negative check — what should not be happening:

CheckWhat wrong looks like

Stomach
Belly hardens, or pulls in. You are bracing your abdominals. Lie down with a hand on
your belly and find a contraction that leaves it still.

Buttocks and thighs
Visible clench, or you rise slightly in your seat. This is the single most common
substitution and it produces nothing.

Breath
You hold it. Holding your breath pushes down with the diaphragm at the same moment you
are trying to lift — the two cancel. Breathe normally; if anything, contract on the
exhale.

If you can produce a contraction that passes all three while the mirror shows movement at the
base of the penis, you have it. Everything else is repetition.

## Where it is, anatomically

The pelvic floor is a hammock of muscle running from the pubic bone at the front to the
tailbone at the back, supporting the bladder and bowel. In men it is a group rather than a
single muscle, and two members of that group do the work this site is about: the
ischiocavernosus and the bulbospongiosus, which sit at the
base of the penis directly on the erectile tissue. When they contract, pressure inside the
erectile bodies rises and venous outflow is restricted — which is the entire mechanism behind
the trial evidence for erectile
function.

That anatomy also explains why the wind cue alone is insufficient. It finds the back of the
hammock. The part that matters here is at the front.

## If you genuinely cannot find it

Two situations worth separating.

You feel nothing at all. Common at the start, and usually a mind-muscle
connection that has simply never been asked for. It typically arrives within a fortnight of
daily attempts. Persistent inability after that is worth an assessment.

You can contract but not release. Different problem, and more important. If
letting go feels effortful or incomplete, or if you have pain, urinary hesitancy or aching
after ejaculation, you may be starting from a pelvic floor that is already too tight — in
which case strengthening is the wrong direction entirely.
What that looks like →

In both cases, one session with a pelvic health physiotherapist replaces a lot of guessing.
They can assess the muscle directly, which is the thing no app, video or article can do.

## Then what

Once the contraction is clean, the programme is straightforward: three sets of eight to
twelve, 3–6 second holds, released for at least as long as you held, progressing from lying to
sitting to standing.

The full protocol and the four mistakes → ·
How long before anything changes →

pelvic floor muscle exercises and manometric biofeedback for erectile dysfunction.
Br J Gen Pract 2004;54(508):819–825.

for male sexual disorders: a narrative review. Int J Impot Res
2025;37:941–949.

## Common questions

Q: How do I know I'm doing kegels right?
A: Three checks. Visually: in a mirror, a correct contraction retracts the base of the penis slightly and lifts the testicles. By touch: a hand on the perineum, between scrotum and anus, feels that area tighten and draw up. By exclusion: nothing else moves — no stomach bracing, no buttock squeeze, no thigh tension, no held breath. The exclusion check catches more errors than the other two combined.

Q: Where exactly are the pelvic floor muscles in men?
A: They form a hammock running from the pubic bone at the front to the tailbone at the back, supporting the bladder and bowel. Two of them, the ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus, sit at the base of the penis directly on the erectile tissue — which is why this muscle group has anything to do with sexual function at all.

Q: Can I feel my pelvic floor from the outside?
A: Yes. Press gently on the perineum — the area between the scrotum and the anus — and contract. You should feel a distinct tightening and a slight drawing upward under your fingers. This is the most useful check for men who cannot tell from sensation alone whether anything is happening.

Q: Why can't I feel my pelvic floor at all?
A: Usually because it has never been consciously used and the mind-muscle connection genuinely isn't there yet — this is normal and improves within a couple of weeks. If it persists, or if you can feel it but cannot release it, that is worth an assessment by a pelvic health physiotherapist rather than more practice.

Q: Should I stop my urine to do kegels?
A: Once, to learn the sensation. Not as a practice method. Regularly interrupting urination can leave residual urine in the bladder and encourage irritation, so it is a diagnostic cue rather than an exercise.

Q: Is it normal to feel it in my abdomen?
A: No, and it is the most common error. If you feel the effort in your stomach, you are bracing your abdominals rather than lifting the pelvic floor. Lie down, put a hand on your belly, and find a contraction that leaves the hand completely still.

# A pelvic floor that is too tight
URL: https://www.vitalityrize.me/hypertonic-pelvic-floor-men/
Language: en
Description: A hypertonic pelvic floor causes pain and hesitancy that look like weakness but are the opposite. How to recognise it, and why kegels make it worse.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: Some men have the opposite of a weak pelvic floor: one that is chronically contracted and cannot fully release. It produces pain in the perineum, penis or testicles, aching after ejaculation, difficulty starting urination and a sense of never fully emptying — and it is routinely mistaken for weakness. Kegels make it worse. What helps is down-training: diaphragmatic breathing, hip and adductor release, heat, and assessment by a pelvic health physiotherapist who can feel what the muscle is doing rather than guess from symptoms.

Every page on this site that recommends pelvic floor training carries the same warning, so
this page exists to give it somewhere to point. Not every pelvic floor problem is weakness. A
meaningful minority of men have the reverse — a muscle group that sits contracted and has
lost the ability to fully let go — and for them the standard advice is not merely useless but
counterproductive.

## Why it gets missed

Pelvic floor advice is written for women after childbirth, where weakness genuinely is the
common problem, and then applied to men unchanged. So a man with pelvic pain reads that he
should squeeze more, squeezes more, feels worse, concludes he isn't trying hard enough, and
squeezes more still. The loop can run for years.

It is also missed clinically. Men in this pattern are frequently treated for prostatitis with
repeated antibiotic courses, because the symptoms overlap and the muscle is not examined.
Bacterial prostatitis is real, but it is a small fraction of men presenting with these
complaints.

## The symptoms

Tension and weakness both produce "something is wrong down there", but they diverge on the
specifics:

Too tight (hypertonic)Too weak (hypotonic)

Pain in perineum, penis, testicles, lower abdomenNo pain

Aching or worse mood after ejaculationEjaculation unremarkable

Hard to start urinating; stop-start streamPost-void dribbling

Feeling of not emptying fullyLeaking on cough, sneeze or lifting

Urgency and frequencyLosing rigidity partway

Pain sitting for long periodsSitting is fine

Worse with stress; worse with more kegelsImproves with kegels

The single most useful discriminator is pain. A weak pelvic floor does not
hurt. If yours does, strengthening is the wrong direction.

Run the eight-question self-check →

## Where the tension comes from

Usually more than one of these at once:

- Stress held physically. The pelvic floor is a guarding muscle; it braces
under threat like the jaw and the shoulders do, and for some people it doesn't unbrace.

- Prolonged sitting, especially with a tucked pelvis, which shortens the
whole complex.

- Over-training. Enthusiastic kegels with no release phase, or heavy lifting
with habitual bracing.

- Protective guarding after pain — a fissure, an infection, an injury — that
outlives the original problem.

- Cycling, in a subset of riders with high saddle pressure and long hours.
The evidence on that is more mixed than the
headlines suggest →

## What actually helps

### 1. Breathe, properly

The diaphragm and pelvic floor move together: the floor descends on the inhale and rises on
the exhale. Most people with chronic pelvic tension breathe shallowly into the chest, which
removes that gentle rhythmic lengthening entirely. Lie down, hand on belly, breathe so the
hand rises, and make the exhale long and unforced. Five minutes, twice a day. This is dull and
it is the single highest-value thing on this page.

### 2. Release the neighbours

Hip flexors, adductors, glutes and the lower back all attach into the same system, and
releasing them reduces the load on the pelvic floor. Happy baby, figure-four, deep squat holds,
and adductor stretching, held long enough to actually let go — 60 to 90 seconds, not 15.

### 3. Heat

Warm baths do more for this than they have any right to. Cheap, safe, and consistently
reported as helpful.

### 4. Reverse kegels — carefully

A reverse kegel is a deliberate lengthening: the gentle sensation of letting go, as if
beginning to urinate, without pushing or straining. Straining is not lengthening and will
make things worse. If you cannot feel the difference between letting go and bearing down,
that is a good reason to see someone rather than to practise harder.

### 5. See a pelvic health physiotherapist

This is the recommendation that matters. A physiotherapist specialising in male pelvic health
can assess the muscle directly rather than inferring it from symptoms, and can do internal
release work that has no home equivalent. Ask a GP for a referral, or search for
"men's pelvic health physiotherapist" in your area. One assessment is worth more than any
quantity of reading, including this page.

## Where VitalityRise fits, and where it doesn't

Honestly: not well, if this is your problem. The app is built around timed contract-and-relax
training, and although every session gives the release its own timed phase and cue, the
programme is a strengthening programme. If your symptoms are pain and hesitancy, it is not the
right tool and we would rather say so than sell you a subscription.

The breathing sessions are the part that transfers. Everything else here needs hands and an
assessment.

Related: reverse kegels, step by step

## Sources

- Sahin E, Brand A, Cetindag EN, Messelink B, Yosmaoglu HB. Pelvic physical therapy
for male sexual disorders: a narrative review. Int J Impot Res
2025;37:941–949.

- Dorey G, Speakman M, Feneley R, et al. Randomised controlled trial of pelvic floor muscle exercises and manometric
biofeedback for erectile dysfunction. Br J Gen Pract 2004;54(508):819–825.

## Common questions

Q: What are the symptoms of a tight pelvic floor in men?
A: Pain or aching in the perineum, penis, testicles or lower abdomen; pain during or after ejaculation; difficulty starting urination or a stop-start stream; a feeling of incomplete emptying; urinary urgency and frequency; pain sitting for long periods; and in some men erectile difficulty or reduced sensation. Pain and hesitancy are the discriminating symptoms — weakness presents as leaking, not as pain.

Q: Can a tight pelvic floor cause erectile dysfunction?
A: It can. A muscle held in permanent partial contraction cannot generate force from a good starting length, and chronic pelvic tension is associated with reduced blood flow and with pain that suppresses arousal in its own right. It is one of the reasons blanket 'do more kegels' advice fails a subset of men and actively harms them.

Q: How do you relax a tight pelvic floor?
A: Down-training rather than strengthening. Diaphragmatic breathing with a long, unforced exhale is the foundation — the pelvic floor descends as the diaphragm does. Add hip flexor, adductor and glute release, warm baths, and deliberate practice at letting go rather than holding. A pelvic health physiotherapist can assess the muscle directly and add internal release work, which is the part you cannot do from a website.

Q: Is a tight pelvic floor the same as chronic pelvic pain syndrome?
A: They overlap heavily. Chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS) is a diagnosis of exclusion in which pelvic floor muscle dysfunction is a recognised component for many men, and pelvic floor physical therapy is part of standard management. If you have been treated with repeated antibiotic courses for 'prostatitis' without improvement, that pattern is worth raising.

Q: How long does it take to release a tight pelvic floor?
A: Longer than strengthening, and less predictably. Men often notice some easing within a few weeks of consistent breathing and stretching work, with meaningful change over months. Progress is rarely linear, and flares under stress are normal rather than a sign of failure.

Q: Should I stop doing kegels?
A: If your symptoms are pain, hesitancy or urgency rather than leaking, yes — stop the strengthening work and shift to release. If you are unsure, the safest position is to train only the relaxation phase and to stop entirely if symptoms worsen over the first fortnight rather than improve.

# Pelvic floor training after prostate surgery
URL: https://www.vitalityrize.me/kegel-exercises-after-prostate-surgery/
Language: en
Description: The largest randomised trial found formal pelvic floor training no better than standard care for incontinence after prostate surgery. What that means.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: This is the one area where the evidence points the other way from the marketing. MAPS, the largest randomised trial, found that formal one-to-one pelvic floor muscle training produced no better continence at 12 months than standard care after radical prostatectomy or TURP. That does not mean the exercises are useless — everyone in both arms was told to do them — it means paying for intensive supervision on top did not add measurable benefit. If you are recovering from prostate surgery, follow the team who operated on you, not an app.

Search for kegels and prostate surgery and you will find a great deal of confident
encouragement, much of it from people selling apps and devices. The best evidence is less
flattering, and since we sell an app ourselves, this page states it plainly.

## What MAPS found

Cathryn Glazener and colleagues ran two parallel randomised controlled trials, published in
The Lancet in 2011, in men with urinary incontinence after radical prostatectomy and
after transurethral resection of the prostate. Men were randomised either to formal
one-to-one pelvic floor muscle training delivered by a therapist, or to
standard care.

At 12 months, both groups had similarly high rates of incontinence. The intensive,
individually taught programme did not beat standard care.

## What that does and does not mean

The result is frequently reported as "kegels don't work after prostate surgery", which
overstates it in one direction, and ignored entirely by the products sold into this market,
which overstates it in the other. Both arms of the trial received the usual post-operative
advice, including pelvic floor instruction. What was randomised was the addition of
formal one-to-one therapy.

So the fair reading is narrow and still important:

- Basic pelvic floor advice remains part of standard post-operative care in most centres.

- Adding intensive supervised training on top did not improve continence at a year.

- Most men recover substantially over that year regardless — which is what makes personal
testimony so unreliable here, and why the trial was needed.

That last point deserves emphasis. When a condition improves on its own over months, anything
you happen to be doing during those months collects the credit. It is the single easiest way
to build a convincing and wrong story about a treatment, and it is the reason "I did kegels
and got better" and "kegels work" are different claims.

## Why we are not the right tool for this

VitalityRise is a general wellness app for men without a specific medical condition. It has
not been tested in post-prostatectomy patients, and neither has any other consumer app in
this category.

Post-surgical recovery differs from general training in ways that matter: timing relative to
catheter removal, what was actually done to your anatomy, whether nerves were spared, and
what your continence baseline is. All of that sits with the team who operated on you. A
timer on a phone knows none of it.

If you were sent home with pelvic floor instructions, follow those. If you were not and want
them, ask your urology team or a specialist pelvic health physiotherapist — that referral is
the useful purchase here, not a subscription.

## What about erections after surgery?

Erectile dysfunction after radical prostatectomy usually stems from damage or trauma to the
cavernous nerves that run alongside the prostate. That is a neural injury, mechanistically
distinct from the veno-occlusive problem that pelvic floor training addresses in men who have
not had surgery. Some reviews describe modest benefit from pelvic floor work within structured
penile rehabilitation programmes, but this is genuinely specialist territory with active
debate about what works, and it is managed alongside PDE5 inhibitors, vacuum devices and
timing decisions that only your urologist can make.

The general evidence on
pelvic floor training and erectile
function comes from men without prostate surgery, and it should not be read across to this
population.

## If you are here for someone else

The genuinely useful things after prostate surgery are unglamorous: follow the surgical
team's protocol, ask for a referral to a pelvic health physiotherapist if incontinence is not
improving on the expected timeline, and know that most improvement happens across the first
year. Continence that has not improved at all by twelve months is a reason to go back and ask
what else is available, because there are surgical options.

## Sources

- Glazener C, Boachie C, Buckley B, et al. Urinary incontinence in men
after formal one-to-one pelvic-floor muscle training following radical prostatectomy or
transurethral resection of the prostate (MAPS): two parallel randomised controlled
trials. Lancet 2011;378(9788):328–337.

- Sahin E, Brand A, Cetindag EN, Messelink B, Yosmaoglu HB. Pelvic physical therapy
for male sexual disorders: a narrative review. Int J Impot Res
2025;37:941–949.

## Common questions

Q: Do kegels help after prostate surgery?
A: Most men regain continence over the months after surgery whether or not they receive formal training, and the largest randomised trial found no difference in continence at 12 months between men given intensive one-to-one pelvic floor training and men given standard care. Basic pelvic floor advice remains part of standard care in most centres; what MAPS tested and did not support was adding formal supervised therapy on top.

Q: What is the MAPS trial?
A: Two parallel randomised controlled trials led by Cathryn Glazener, published in The Lancet in 2011, testing formal one-to-one pelvic floor muscle training against standard care for urinary incontinence after radical prostatectomy and after transurethral resection of the prostate. It reported similar high rates of incontinence at 12 months in both groups.

Q: How long does incontinence last after prostatectomy?
A: It is usual immediately after surgery and improves over months, with most recovery in the first year. Because that natural improvement is substantial, it is easy to attribute it to whatever you happened to be doing at the time — which is exactly why a randomised comparison was needed and why its result surprised people.

Q: Should I use a kegel app after prostate surgery?
A: We would not recommend ours for it. Post-surgical rehabilitation is a clinical situation with a specific timeline, specific precautions and a surgical team who know what was done to your anatomy. A general fitness app built for a healthy population is not the right instrument, and no consumer app in this category has been tested in post-prostatectomy patients.

Q: Can pelvic floor exercises help erections after prostate surgery?
A: Erectile dysfunction after radical prostatectomy is usually caused by damage to the cavernous nerves running alongside the prostate, which is a different mechanism from the venous and muscular ones pelvic floor training addresses. Some reviews report modest benefit as part of penile rehabilitation programmes, but this is a specialist area and the right people to ask are the urology team managing your recovery.

Q: Does this mean pelvic floor training doesn't work at all?
A: No, and the distinction matters. MAPS tested one specific thing — added formal therapy for post-surgical incontinence — in one specific population. The trials supporting pelvic floor training for erectile dysfunction in men without prostate surgery are separate, and they were positive.
